fields.definition: A self-contained mobile facility, typically a van, truck, or trailer, fitted with mixing consoles, recorders, communications, and transmission links to capture and produce audio programming at a remote site away from the studio. It is the audio-focused member of a broadcaster's outside-broadcast (OB) fleet, used for sports, concerts, and live events.
fields.plain_english: It is a truck or van packed with audio gear. A crew drives it to a game or concert. From inside, they mix the sound and send it back to the station.
fields.purpose_function: It brings a full studio's worth of audio production and transmission capability to events that cannot come to the studio, letting a broadcaster originate live or recorded programming from the field.
fields.practical_application: A radio engineer parks the vehicle at a stadium, patches microphone and stage feeds into its console, and sends the finished mix back to the station over an IP, ISDN, or satellite link.
common_mistakes: Confusing an audio-only OB vehicle with a full television OB truck, which also carries video switching and camera systems
Assuming the vehicle needs no independent power and grounding plan once parked on site
UNSAFE: Powering the vehicle from an unverified venue mains outlet without checking grounding and bonding, risking shock and equipment damage
scenario_contexts: Broadcasting live match commentary from a stadium car park
Producing a multi-day music festival radio show from the site
Covering breaking news from a remote location where no studio exists

sources: EBU technical guidelines on contribution and remote production

fields.definition: An operating mode of a radio broadcast automation (playout) system in which a live operator manually triggers and sequences programme elements, such as songs, jingles, adverts, and links, while the software handles file loading, logging, and playback. It sits between fully manual live operation and fully unattended automation, keeping a human in control of timing and content.
fields.plain_english: The computer lines up the songs and ads for the show. But a person clicks to play each one. So the show feels live, with a human in charge of the timing.
fields.purpose_function: It lets a presenter drive a live-sounding show while keeping the log accuracy and safety net of automation, so timing and content stay under human control and the system does the file handling.
fields.practical_application: A daytime presenter runs the show in assist mode, hitting play-next after each song so links land naturally, then switches the system to full automation when leaving for the night.
common_mistakes: Believing elements fire on time by themselves; in assist mode items only play when the operator triggers them, so inattention causes dead air
Confusing live-assist with voice tracking, where links are pre-recorded rather than performed live
Forgetting that the on-air log still records what actually played, so skipped adverts create reconciliation problems
scenario_contexts: A live morning show where the host controls timing around traffic and news
Dropping a live sports result into an otherwise automated schedule
Training a new presenter to drive the playout system before trusting full automation

sources: Radio automation/playout system technical manuals (e.g., ENCO, RCS, WideOrbit)

fields.definition: A secondary audio source held ready to feed the air chain when the primary programme feed fails, ranging from an emergency playout of stored content to an alternate studio, satellite, or network feed. It is selected automatically by a changeover or silence-sensing device, or manually by an operator, to prevent dead air.
fields.plain_english: It is a spare source of sound for the station. If the main feed dies, the station switches to it. This stops silence from going out on air.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to keep programming on the air during a failure of the main source, protecting against dead air that can breach licence conditions and drive listeners away.
fields.practical_application: An engineer loads several hours of evergreen music onto an emergency player and wires it to a silence sensor so it takes over automatically if the studio feed drops.
common_mistakes: Never testing the backup source, so it fails when it is finally needed
Routing the backup through the same failure-prone path (same server or link) as the primary
Assuming automatic changeover repairs the primary; someone must still fix it and switch back
scenario_contexts: Studio automation crashes overnight and the backup player keeps music on air
A satellite network feed drops and the station falls back to local content
A silence sensor detects dead air and switches to the emergency source

fields.definition: A monitoring and warning system in a broadcast facility that detects fault conditions in the air chain, such as prolonged silence (dead air), loss of carrier, over-modulation, or transmitter faults, and alerts staff or triggers automatic corrective action. It typically combines silence sensors, remote-control telemetry, and audible, visual, or messaging alerts.
fields.plain_english: It watches the station's sound and gear for problems. If the air goes silent or a fault appears, it warns the staff. Some systems can even switch to a backup on their own.
fields.purpose_function: It protects continuity of service by catching failures, especially dead air, quickly, so staff can respond before listeners are lost or licence rules are broken.
fields.practical_application: An engineer sets a silence sensor to trigger after a few seconds of quiet, sending a text alert and switching to the backup source automatically.
common_mistakes: Setting silence thresholds so tight that quiet passages of programme trigger false alarms
UNSAFE: Bypassing or muting transmitter fault alarms to stop nuisance alerts, masking conditions that can damage the transmitter or breach RF exposure limits
Relying on alarms that nobody monitors outside office hours
scenario_contexts: Overnight unattended operation where alarms are the only line of defence
Detecting a stuck audio feed that has gone silent
Warning staff of a transmitter power fault at a remote site

sources: Silence-monitor/remote-control manufacturer technical manuals (e.g., Broadcast Tools, DEVA)

fields.definition: A networked storage system that ingests, catalogues, and retains broadcast audio, including finished programmes, raw recordings, and continuous off-air logs, for reuse, repurposing, and regulatory compliance. It provides searchable, often long-term storage kept separate from the fast online storage used for daily playout.
fields.plain_english: It is a big storage computer for a station's audio. It keeps old shows and recordings in an organized way. Staff can search it and pull files back when they need them.
fields.purpose_function: It preserves programme material and legally required recordings so content can be found and reused later, while keeping the active playout storage free for current work.
fields.practical_application: A producer searches the archive server for a past interview, retrieves the file, and re-edits it into a new feature.
common_mistakes: Treating the archive as a backup; it stores masters, but without a second copy it is not disaster-proof
Failing to enter consistent metadata, which makes files impossible to find later
Ignoring the retention period that regulators require for off-air logs
scenario_contexts: Retrieving a broadcast recording to answer a listener complaint or regulator request
Repurposing archived material into a highlights programme
Meeting a legal duty to retain recordings of everything aired

sources: EBU technical documentation on production storage and archiving

fields.definition: A recorder or recording system that captures immersive Dolby Atmos audio, meaning channel beds plus object-based elements carrying positional metadata, for broadcast and streaming production. It stores the multichannel audio together with its metadata so the immersive mix can be reproduced and re-rendered downstream.
fields.plain_english: It records surround sound that can also come from above you. It saves the sound plus data about where each sound sits. This lets the full 3D mix play back later.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to capture immersive, object-based audio for programmes made in Dolby Atmos, keeping the audio and its positional metadata intact through the production chain.
fields.practical_application: An audio engineer on a live concert broadcast records the Atmos bed and objects so the immersive mix can be finished and delivered for streaming.
common_mistakes: Recording only the channel bed and losing the object metadata, which collapses the immersive mix
Assuming an Atmos recording folds down to stereo automatically without checking the downmix
Confusing Dolby Atmos with plain 5.1 surround, which has no height or object layer
scenario_contexts: Capturing an immersive mix of a live orchestral broadcast
Recording sports crowd atmosphere in Atmos for a streaming platform
Delivering an Atmos programme master for on-demand playback

sources: AES and SMPTE material on object-based/immersive audio

fields.definition: A mixing console designed for on-air broadcast use, combining program and audition (off-air) buses, mix-minus outputs, telephone and codec integration, and monitor-muting/tally logic for the studio. It routes and mixes microphones, playout, and remote sources into the station's programme feed.
fields.plain_english: It is the mixing desk in a radio studio. It blends mics, music, and phone callers into one feed for air. It also mutes the studio speakers when a mic is live, to stop feedback.
fields.purpose_function: It is the central point where all studio and remote audio is combined, leveled, and routed to air, adding broadcast-specific features such as mix-minus and mic-triggered monitor muting.
fields.practical_application: A presenter opens their mic fader, brings up a music bed, and takes a phone caller on a mix-minus bus so the caller does not hear their own delayed voice.
common_mistakes: Sending a caller or remote guest a full mix instead of mix-minus, causing echo or feedback
Ignoring monitor-muting logic and creating howl-round when the studio mic is live over the speakers
Confusing the audition/cue bus with the program bus and putting off-air content to air
scenario_contexts: Running a live phone-in show with multiple callers
Mixing a live music session in the on-air studio
Handing a remote OB feed onto air through the console

sources: Broadcast console manufacturer technical documentation (e.g., Wheatstone/Axia, Lawo, Calrec)

fields.definition: A crosspoint routing system that connects many audio sources to many destinations in a broadcast facility, letting any input be assigned to any output under operator or automation control. Modern implementations are commonly networked over AES67 audio-over-IP, distributing signals across studios, playout, and transmission paths.
fields.plain_english: It is a big audio switchboard for the station. It can send any source to any place. Staff pick which input goes to which output, by hand or by software.
fields.purpose_function: It provides flexible, central signal distribution so any source can reach any studio, processor, or transmitter path without repatching physical cables.
fields.practical_application: An engineer uses the router control panel to send the incoming satellite network feed to Studio 2's console and to the transmitter path at the same time.
common_mistakes: Making a routing change on air without checking which destinations are live, cutting a source off air
Assuming a salvo or preset recalls levels as well as routes when it may only recall crosspoints
Confusing an audio matrix with a mixing console; a matrix routes but does not mix or blend levels
scenario_contexts: Distributing a shared network feed to several studios at once
Switching the transmitter feed from the main studio to a backup studio
Routing remote OB returns to the correct production room

fields.definition: A dedicated production room and its equipment, including a digital audio workstation, calibrated monitoring, and processing, used to edit, mix, and finish audio for broadcast programmes after acquisition. Work includes dialogue editing, sound design, music, and a loudness-compliant final mix that meets the broadcaster's delivery specifications.
fields.plain_english: It is an editing room for finishing a show's sound. Staff clean up speech, add music and effects, and set the loudness. The result is ready to broadcast.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to turn raw recorded material into a polished, loudness-compliant final mix that meets the broadcaster's technical delivery standards.
fields.practical_application: An audio editor cuts the dialogue for a documentary in the post suite, adds effects and music, then mixes to the required loudness target before delivery.
common_mistakes: Mixing to peak level instead of the required integrated loudness target, so the programme is rejected or re-leveled
Monitoring at inconsistent levels, leading to dialogue that is too quiet or too loud on air
Delivering in the wrong file format or channel layout for the broadcaster's specification
scenario_contexts: Finishing the audio mix of a radio drama or documentary
Editing and sweetening a pre-recorded interview before transmission
Mixing a programme to EBU R128 or ATSC A/85 loudness compliance
